title: Adjectives and demonstratives

objectives.can: Match an adjective or demonstrative to its noun, and tell the attributive from the predicate use.

explanation.summary: A Hebrew adjective agrees with its noun in gender, number and definiteness, and it follows the noun. 'This' and 'that' behave in the same way. The article decides whether the adjective is 'the great light' or a statement that the light is great.

sections.heading: Adjectives agree with their noun
body: An adjective has the same four forms as a noun of its kind: masculine and feminine, singular and plural. The feminine singular is usually -ָה and the masculine plural usually -ִים, as with nouns. So the adjective טוֹב, 'good', is טוֹבָה with a feminine noun and טוֹבִים with masculine plural nouns. Whatever the noun is, the adjective takes the same gender and number.
The two paradigms below are made by the build from the forms the texts really hold. A dash means that this form does not occur in these texts, not that it cannot exist.

sections.heading: The attributive adjective
body: An attributive adjective is part of a noun phrase: 'the great light', 'a good old age'. In Hebrew it stands after its noun and agrees with it in gender, number and also in definiteness. If the noun has the article, the adjective has it too: הַמָּאוֹר הַגָּדֹל, 'the great light'. If the noun is indefinite, so is the adjective: בְּשֵׂיבָה טוֹבָה, 'in a good old age'.
When a noun has more than one adjective, each follows and agrees in the same way.

sections.heading: The predicate adjective
body: A predicate adjective makes a statement about the noun: 'the tree is good'. Hebrew has no word for 'is' in such a clause. The adjective has no article, and it often (not always) comes first: טוֹב הָעֵץ, 'good (is) the tree'. The adjective still agrees with its noun in gender and number.

So you can tell the two uses apart by the article. An adjective with the article after a noun with the article is attributive. An adjective without the article beside a noun that has it is predicate. When both lack the article, context decides, and often word order too.

sections.heading: 'This' and 'these', 'that' and 'those'
body: The demonstratives are זֶה, 'this' (masculine singular), זֹאת, 'this' (feminine singular), and אֵלֶּה, 'these' (one form for both genders). Used with a noun they follow it and take the article together with the noun: הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה, הָאָרֶץ הַזֹּאת, 'this day, this land'. On their own they work like pronouns: זֹאת הַפַּעַם, 'this time'.

Hebrew has no separate word for 'that'. It uses the third person pronouns, הוּא, הִיא, הֵם, הֵנָּה, with the article after the noun: בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא, 'on that day', and בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם, 'in those days'. In the word display these are tagged as personal pronouns (with Definite), not as demonstratives, but they are used as 'that' and 'those'.

head: Meaning
Masculine singular
Feminine singular
Plural
rows: this, these, with the noun's article
that, those, with the noun's article

misunderstandings: The adjective does not come before the noun, as in English. The usual order is noun, then adjective: in הַמָּאוֹר הַגָּדֹל the word for 'light' comes first and 'great' second.
An article on the adjective does not mean that the adjective is a separate noun. When it repeats the noun's article, it is part of the same phrase.
The adjective in טוֹב הָעֵץ has no article, and this is not a mistake or a missing word. The missing article, together with the absence of a verb, is what makes it a statement.
הוּא is 'he' or 'it' as a subject, and 'that' only after a noun with the article. In הַיּוֹם הַהוּא it means 'that', not 'he'.

deeper.heading: Adjectives used as nouns
body: An adjective can stand with no noun and mean a person or thing of that kind: צַדִּיק can be 'a righteous person', and the headword זָקֵן is often 'an old man', 'an elder'. The word display tags such words as adjectives whenever the form is that of an adjective, and the context of a verse shows whether a noun is understood.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And God made the two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night; and the stars.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: הַגָּדֹל follows its noun הַמָּאוֹר and has the article as it does: masculine singular, 'the great light'. In the next clause הַקָּטֹן does the same with the same noun, 'the small light'. These are attributive adjectives.

quoted.english: And when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat; and she gave also unto her husband with her, and he did eat.

examples.analysis: טוֹב has no article and comes before הָעֵץ, which has one: 'good (was) the tree'. This is a predicate adjective, with no verb 'to be' in the clause. The adjective is masculine singular, like עֵץ.

examples.analysis: Three phrases with the article on both words. בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא is 'on that day': הַהוּא is the pronoun 'he' used as 'that'. הָאָרֶץ הַזֹּאת is 'this land': זֹאת is a feminine singular demonstrative. הַנָּהָר הַגָּדֹל is 'the great river': an attributive adjective.
